newsitem.title: UK: Multinational force still needed for Zaire - envoy.
newsitem.headline: Multinational force still needed for Zaire - envoy.

text.p: U.N. special envoy Raymond Chretien said on Sunday a multinational humanitarian force was still needed in troubled eastern Zaire despite the fact tens of thousands of Hutu refugees were returning to Rwanda.

"I can see the need for such a force...Don't think only of what you see on the television screens. There is a huge number of refugees that are absolutely invisible but are still very much in eastern Zaire," Chretien said in a BBC radio interview.
He was speaking from Rwanda's capital Kigali where he was holding talks with Rwandan leaders as part of his shuttle diplomacy in the volatile central African region.
Chretien said he had discussed the current return of Hutu refugees with Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu.
"I reminded him of course that what we are witnessing is very positive news. This is what they've have been looking for for years," said Chretien.
"However, there is approximately 1.2 million refugees in eastern Zaire and so far just a very small percentage of that huge number have come back.
"So we will have to see in the days to come what happens on the ground and then clearly take that into account in the organisation of that (multinational) force."

The multinational force would probably be involved in working out a strategy to "reach the refugees wherever they are in eastern Zaire -- to feed them, take care of them and bring them back to their countries of origin".
The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR said on Saturday a total of 200,000 Rwandan Hutus among the more than one million who fled to Zaire in 1994 had so far returned since Friday.

The mass exodus began suddenly on Friday when an alliance of Zairean rebels forced Hutu militiamen, who had been preventing the refugees from leaving, to flee the teeming camps they had ruthlessly controlled since 1994.

The militia and former Hutu government troops had spearheaded the genocide of some one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994, before being driven out by Tutsi rebels who went on to establish a new government in Kigali.

The flood of refugees back to Rwanda prompted U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry to say the rapidly changing situation could force a change in plans for the Canadian-led multinational force that the U.N. Security Council approved by a unanimous vote on Friday.
Perry told a news conference in Washington on Saturday the United States would consult its allies after receiving a report this weekend from a survey team in the region.
Rwandan leaders said the mass return of Hutus meant the multinational force was obsolete before it was even deployed and the world should send aid instead to help Rwanda settle the refugees.
